clinician.final_diagnosis: severe bilateral necrotising retinopathy from ophthalmic shingles in the setting of unrecognised long-standing HIV infection
clinician.trajectory_summary: A retired woman with a history of left-sided herpes zoster ophthalmicus and keratouveitis presented with a 4-week reduction of right vision. Initial ophthalmological examination of the right eye revealed vitreous haze, multiple areas of white retinal swelling in the posterior pole with macula involvement, and obliterated arterioles with perivascular sheathing. Left eye funduscopy was precluded by cataract, but showed diffuse stromal corneal scarring and posterior synechiae. Ultrasound confirmed bilateral retinal detachments. Workup revealed HIV positive status with severe immunosuppression (viral load 116,912 copies/mL and CD4 T lymphocyte count 37 cells/µL). Aqueous humor PCR from the right eye was positive for VZV DNA and negative for CMV and herpes simplex. The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous acyclovir, oral valacyclovir, intravitreal foscarnet, and commenced antiretroviral therapy. Despite treatment, vision remained no perception of light in both eyes, and bilateral retinal detachments were considered inoperable, leading to the patient being registered blind.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with 4-week reduction of right vision and a history of left-sided herpes zoster ophthalmicus and keratouveitis.

Right eye funduscopy showed vitreous haze, multiple areas of white retinal swelling in the posterior pole with macula involvement, and obliterated arterioles with perivascular sheathing (Kyrieleis’ plaques).
Left eye had diffuse stromal corneal scarring, long-standing pigmented keratic precipitates, and 360 degrees posterior synechiae, with funduscopy precluded by cataract.
Patient was HIV positive with a viral load of 116,912 copies/mL and a CD4 T lymphocyte count of 37 cells/µL.
Aqueous from anterior chamber paracentesis of the right eye was positive for VZV DNA on PCR.
Patient received treatment including IV acyclovir, oral valacyclovir, intravitreal foscarnet, and commenced antiretroviral therapy.
Vision remained no perception of light in both eyes, and bilateral retinal detachments were considered inoperable, leading to the patient being registered blind.
